description:
The stale-binary provenance guard refuses to run gates whenever the repository's `HEAD` differs from the installed binary's build commit, even when the intervening changes cannot affect the compiled binary. Scope the guard so only changes to the binary's actual build inputs invalidate it.

## Background

The installed `jit` binary embeds build provenance — the git commit it was built from and whether that build tree was dirty — injected at install time by the provenance-injecting install wrapper around `cargo install`. Before running any `exec` gate checker, the evaluator (and any `jit` process a checker itself spawns) compares that embedded build commit against the repository's current `HEAD`. When the build commit is a commit the repository's history contains and it no longer equals `HEAD` (or the recorded build was dirty), the guard refuses to run the gate and directs the operator to rebuild and reinstall.

The refusal is correct in intent: a gate verdict produced by a binary that predates the tree under review is not evidence about that tree. The problem is the comparison — raw commit-hash equality against `HEAD`. Ordinary workflow commits move `HEAD` without touching any compiled source: claiming an issue commits `.jit/` state, linking a plan document, refreshing a projection. Each such commit trips the guard and forces a full rebuild-and-reinstall before any gate can run again, even though the installed binary is still the correct build for the source under review. In a single planning session this compounds into repeated rebuild cycles for commits that changed only repository data or documentation.

The build itself already ignores non-source metadata for reproducibility: staging or committing unchanged sources does not make the binary non-fresh. The guard should reach the same conclusion — a `HEAD` move that leaves the binary's sources unchanged must not invalidate the binary.

The identity predicate that keeps the guard silent for unrelated repositories — the build commit must be a commit the repository's history actually contains — is already correct and independent of this change; it must be preserved.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The guard treats the installed binary as current when every difference between its build commit and the tree under review — both committed and uncommitted — is confined to paths that cannot affect the compiled `jit` binary (for example `.jit/` data and documentation), so a `HEAD`-moving commit that changes only such paths does not cause a gate refusal.
- [hard] REQ-02: The guard refuses to run the gate, with the existing actionable rebuild-and-reinstall message and its unchanged pre-verdict exit code (10), whenever any difference between the build commit and the tree under review touches a build-input path (Rust crate sources, or the Cargo manifests and lockfile that determine the binary).
- [hard] REQ-03: Uncommitted working-tree changes to build-input paths cause a refusal even when `HEAD` still equals the build commit; a working tree whose only uncommitted changes are outside build-input paths does not cause a refusal.
- [hard] REQ-04: A binary whose recorded build was dirty is still treated as stale, preserving current dirty-build handling — a dirty build has no commit that fully describes its sources.
- [hard] REQ-05: The guard stays silent, never refusing, when the repository does not contain the binary's build commit, when there is no resolvable `HEAD`, or when there is no git; an ordinary installed release validating an unrelated repository is unaffected.
- [hard] REQ-06: The set of build-input paths reflects what actually compiles into the binary rather than a hand-maintained denylist of known-safe directories, so introducing a new top-level path that the binary does not compile (for example a new documentation or tooling directory) does not by itself cause the guard to refuse.

## Notes

The scoped behavior must apply identically at both enforcement sites that share the provenance comparison: the evaluator's guard that runs before it spawns a checker, and the startup self-check of a `jit` process spawned by a checker that resolves its own binary independently. Both the commit-mismatch and dirty-build refusal messages remain unchanged in wording and exit code; only the condition that decides whether to refuse is narrowed to build-input differences.
title: Scope the stale-binary provenance guard to build-input changes
